1.pericope_label: Thus hath the Lord God shewed unto me; and, behold, he formed grasshoppers in the beginning of the shooting up of the latter growth; and, lo, it was the latter growth after the king’s mowings. And it came to pass, that when they had made an end of eating the grass of the land, then I said, O Lord God, forgive, I beseech thee: by whom shall Jacob arise? for he is small. The Lord repented for this: It shall not be, saith the Lord
debates: What historical affliction the locusts stand for
How the plea for Jacob should be rendered
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch pairs the visions by whether intercession is answered
Ellicott calls the received rendering of the prophet’s plea incorrect
Clarke reports a reading that makes the mowings a shearing of the king’s sheep
themes: A second growth eaten before it can be harvested
An ant built with as much skill as an elephant
A land wasted without its people looking up
A purpose changed without a mind changing

4.pericope_label: Thus hath the Lord God shewed unto me: and, behold, the Lord God called to contend by fire, and it devoured the great deep, and did eat up a part. Then said I, O Lord God, cease, I beseech thee: by whom shall Jacob arise? for he is small. The Lord repented for this: This also shall not be, saith the Lord God
debates: Whether the fire is war or a figure of drought
What the devoured great deep means
Why the same judgment is threatened and withdrawn twice
outliers: Calvin makes the two visions a rule about how God escalates punishment
Ellicott denies that the great deep can mean the heathen world
Calvin says deferred punishment is not a threat made in vain
themes: Fire called down on land already stripped
A prairie burning what the locusts left
Springs of water scorched at their source
Patience mistaken for emptiness

7.pericope_label: Thus he shewed me: and, behold, the Lord stood upon a wall made by a plumbline, with a plumbline in his hand. And the Lord said unto me, Amos, what seest thou? And I said, A plumbline. Then said the Lord, Behold, I will set a plumbline in the midst of my people Israel: I will not again pass by them any more: And the high places of Isaac shall be desolate, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste
debates: Why the prophet does not intercede a third time
Which high places of Isaac are meant
outliers: Calvin calls almost all the ingenious readings of the plumbline frigid
Ellicott notes that a plumb-line serves for dismantling as well as building
Clarke traces the threat against the royal house to a promise made four generations earlier
themes: A wall measured by the tool that built it
A prophet struck silent by what he sees
A door of mercy shut against later prayers
An altar of the fathers turned to laughter

10.pericope_label: Then Amaziah the priest of Beth-el sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, Amos hath conspired against thee in the midst of the house of Israel: the land is not able to bear all his words. Also Amaziah said unto Amos, O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there: But prophesy not again any more at Beth-el: for it is the king’s chapel, and it is the king’s court
debates: What moved the priest to lay an information
Whether the report of the prophecy was accurate
Why no answer from the king is recorded
outliers: Clarke says there is not one word of truth in the priest’s message
Calvin reads the offer of escape and the threat of danger as two engines used together
Ellicott finds evidence here that the preaching had been felt in the palaces as well as the sanctuary
themes: A shrine that would be deserted if the preaching held
A sword threatened against a house, not a man
A silence where an answer was expected
An ape appearing at last as the ape

14.pericope_label: Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet’s son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit: And the Lord took me as I followed the flock, and the Lord said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel. Therefore thus saith the Lord; Thy wife shall be an harlot in the city, and thy sons and thy daughters shall fall by the sword, and thou shalt die in a polluted land
debates: Why the prophet begins by denying that he is one
What the gathering of sycomore fruit involved
Whether the sentence punishes the idolatry or the interference
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch reads the denial as refusing the charge of prophesying for a living
Ellicott doubts the ancient custom of pinching figs is what the Hebrew word means
Calvin says the doom falls for opposing God’s authority, not for false worship alone
themes: A calling taken up under compulsion
Figs pinched to make them ripen
A prohibition answered with a formula
Bread eaten outside the land and counted unclean
